Are Ontario’s Municipalities Meeting Their Housing Targets?

An inferential analysis of provincial housing-supply progress, 2023–2024

Your Name

November 04, 2026

Key findings

  1. Most municipalities are falling short, and 2024 was weaker than 2023. Only 20 of 50 municipalities exceeded their annual target in 2023 and 15 in 2024; 18 and 25 respectively were below 80% (“Not met”). The 50 targeted municipalities together reached 96.7% of their combined target in 2023 and 74.2% in 2024.
  2. The average municipality is statistically indistinguishable from 100%. Mean attainment was 120.5% (2023; 95% CI [89.8, 151.1]) and 97.7% (2024; 95% CI [73.9, 121.6]). Both intervals contain 100% (p = 0.186 and 0.849), and bootstrap intervals agree. The unweighted mean is pulled up by a few small municipalities (median: 88.5% and 78.4%).
  3. The 2023→2024 drop (22.7 percentage points on average) is borderline. The paired t-test (p = 0.072) and Wilcoxon test (p = 0.070) do not reach the 5% level, while a bootstrap interval for the mean change, [0.2, 48.8], only just excludes zero. Province-wide, units fell 12.7% while annual targets rose 13.6%, so the lower attainment reflects both forces.
  4. Bigger targets are associated with lower attainment. In a log-log regression, doubling a municipality’s annual target is associated with about 16% lower attainment in 2023 (slope -0.252, 95% CI [-0.406, -0.098], p = 0.002), and the pattern repeats in 2024. The result survives dropping either Toronto or Chatham-Kent (the most extreme observations) and is confirmed by bootstrap.
  5. Cross-validation confirms the relationship is real but modest. Repeated 5-fold CV shows the log-log model cutting out-of-sample RMSE by about 14.0% relative to predicting the average, whereas the raw linear model is worse than the baseline in repeated CV.

1 Background and research questions

1.1 Policy context

Ontario has a goal of building at least 1.5 million homes by 2031, backed by measures such as the More Homes Built Faster Act, 2022. To pursue it, the province assigned a ten-year housing target (2022–2031) to each of its 50 largest and fastest-growing municipalities, based on current population and 2011–2021 growth trends. Each ten-year target is broken into annual calendar-year targets that ramp up until 2026. Toronto, for example, carries the largest target: 285,000 homes.

1.2 Who collected the data, and how

The data come from the Ontario Data Catalogue dataset Ontario’s housing supply progress, published under the Open Government Licence – Ontario by the provincial Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing (the dataset is maintained by its Planning Policy Branch and updated monthly). It counts how many new homes were started toward each municipal target in a calendar year. For 2023 this includes housing starts, additional residential units (e.g. secondary suites) and long-term-care beds; from 2024 it also includes postsecondary student beds and licensed congregate retirement-home suites. The published figures reflect the ministry’s post-review adjustments and may differ from CMHC’s Starts and Completions Survey. I use the two annual files (January–December 2023 and 2024) as last updated in December 2025.

Three features matter for interpretation:

  • The unit counted is a housing start, not a completion, so “progress” below means attainment of the annual start target.
  • The 2024 count has a broader definition than 2023 (student beds, retirement suites), so year-over-year comparisons are only approximately like-for-like.
  • Annual targets rise over time, so a lower attainment percentage can reflect higher targets and not only fewer homes.

1.3 Research questions

  1. Are municipalities meeting their annual housing targets? (How many exceed, are on track, or fall short, in each year?)
  2. What is the average attainment rate, and is it different from the 100% goal? Did it change between 2023 and 2024?
  3. Is the size of a municipality’s target related to how much of it is achieved?

2 Data

2.1 Variables

After cleaning, the analysis uses one row per municipality (n = 50) with the variables below. The attainment rate is the official “Progress %”: units started in the year divided by the annual target, times 100, so 100% means the target was exactly met.

Table 1. Data dictionary (cleaned data).
Variable Type Range Description
municipality text 50 municipalities Municipality name
ten_year_target integer 1,000 – 285,000 Homes required by 2031 (2022–2031), province-assigned
annual_target_YYYY integer 73 – 23,750 Province-assigned target for calendar year YYYY (2023 or 2024)
annual_units_YYYY integer 60 – 31,656 New homes started in year YYYY
progress_pct_YYYY numeric 11.1 – 644.4 Attainment rate: 100 × units ÷ annual target (stored as text with a % sign in the raw file)
status_YYYY factor Not met / On track / Exceeded Not met (< 80%), On track (80% to < 100%), Exceeded (≥ 100%)
size_class factor (derived) 4 levels Ten-year target: Small < 5k, Medium 5–20k, Large 20–60k, Major ≥ 60k

2.2 Cleaning and validation

The raw files each contain 51 rows. Three issues were handled explicitly:

  • Aggregate row removed. The last row, Municipalities without targets, is the combined total of all other Ontario municipalities, not a municipality. Treating it as a 51st observation would distort every mean, test and model, so it is excluded from all municipal-level analysis (it is used only for the province-wide totals in Section 3.1).
  • Whitespace. The 2024 file spells one name "Woodstock " with a trailing space; left alone, joining the two years silently drops that municipality. Names are trimmed before merging.
  • Text to numbers. Percentages stored as text ("89.90%") are parsed to numeric.
Table 2. Automated data-quality checks.
Check Result
Published % equals units ÷ annual target (±0.05 pp) Pass
Published status follows the 80% / 100% rule Pass
Cumulative 2024 − 2024 units = cumulative 2023 (all 50) Pass
Municipality names unique after trimming whitespace Pass

3 Descriptive analysis

3.1 Are targets being met?

Table 3. Aggregate attainment: total units started ÷ total annual targets.
Year Units started (50 targeted municipalities) Annual targets (50) Attainment (50) Attainment, all Ontario municipalities
2023 94,090 97,337 96.7% 100.3%
2024 82,106 110,610 74.2% 75.9%

Taken together, the 50 targeted municipalities achieved 96.7% of their combined 2023 target but only 74.2% in 2024. Counting every Ontario municipality (including those without targets) gives 100.3% and 75.9%. Total units started fell by 12.7% while the summed annual targets rose by 13.6%, so both forces pushed the 2024 attainment down.

The share of municipalities that fell short (< 80% of target) rose from 36% (18 of 50) in 2023 to 50% (25) in 2024, while the number exceeding their target fell from 20 to 15.

Table 4. Status transition matrix: how each municipality’s status changed (n = 50).
2023 status ↓ / 2024 status → Not met On track Exceeded
Not met 12 4 2
On track 6 4 2
Exceeded 7 2 11

27 of the 50 municipalities kept the same status. The most common move was from Exceeded to Not met (7 municipalities), compared with only 2 moving the other way, so performance was far from stable at the individual level. Strong results one year did not predict strong results the next.

3.2 Distribution of attainment

Both distributions are strongly right-skewed: most municipalities cluster between roughly 25% and 150% of target, with a thin tail of high performers (Chatham-Kent at 644.4% in 2023; North Bay at 479.5% in 2024). In 2023 the tallest bar sits just below the 100% line; in 2024 the mass shifts left.

Table 5. The five highest and five lowest attainment rates in each year.
Rank 2023 – highest 2023 – lowest 2024 – highest 2024 – lowest
1 Chatham-Kent (644.4%) Halton Hills (20.7%) North Bay (479.5%) Whitchurch-Stouffville (11.1%)
2 Sarnia (347.9%) New Tecumseth (21.5%) Chatham-Kent (338.0%) Ajax (19.1%)
3 Belleville (307.1%) Burlington (27.5%) Greater Sudbury (265.0%) Newmarket (22.3%)
4 North Bay (276.7%) Newmarket (32.5%) Windsor (212.9%) Aurora (28.3%)
5 Welland (275.6%) Windsor (36.3%) Sarnia (197.6%) Woodstock (29.3%)

The highest rates mostly belong to municipalities with very small targets (Chatham-Kent, Sarnia, North Bay and Belleville each have ten-year targets of about 1,000–3,100 homes), where a few hundred extra homes translate into a very large percentage. At the other end, the largest targets do not produce the highest rates: Mississauga (ten-year target 120,000) reached only 39.4% of its target in 2023 and 35.0% in 2024.

3.3 Summary statistics

Table 6. Summary statistics of attainment rate (%), by year.
Year n Mean Median SD IQR Min Max Share ≥ 100%
2023 50 120.5 88.5 107.8 86.7 20.7 644.4 40
2024 50 97.7 78.4 83.8 68.1 11.1 479.5 30

Reading Table 6. In both years the mean exceeds the median (120.5 vs 88.5 in 2023; 97.7 vs 78.4 in 2024), which is the numerical signature of right skew: a handful of extreme values drag the mean upward, so the median describes the typical municipality better. The typical municipality reached only about 88% of its target in 2023 and 78% in 2024, i.e. it fell short both years. The spread is large relative to the centre (SD 107.8 and 83.8), and the full range runs from 11.1% to 644.4%. Between years, the mean dropped by 22.7 points, the median by 10.1, and the share of municipalities at or above 100% fell from 40% to 30%, a consistent downward shift. Spread also narrowed (SD down by 23.9), largely because the 2023 maximum was more extreme than any 2024 value.

Reading Figure 3. Both boxes sit below the 100% line at the median, with the 2024 box shifted down and compressed relative to 2023. Both have long upper whiskers and several outliers above the whiskers (the extreme points identified in Table 5), confirming the right skew seen in the histograms. The two distributions overlap heavily: most of the 2024 box lies within the range of the 2023 box, a first hint that the year-to-year shift is modest compared with the variation between municipalities, which the formal comparison in Section 4.2 tests.

3.4 Attainment by municipality size

Table 7. Attainment rate (%) by municipality size class.
Size class n Mean 2023 Median 2023 Mean 2024 Median 2024
Small (<5k) 11 235.9 193.6 185.5 143.2
Medium (5-20k) 24 91.6 84.6 72.3 53.7
Large (20-60k) 11 78.2 67.3 78.6 69.5
Major (60k+) 4 92.2 89.0 61.9 62.0

Small municipalities (ten-year target under 5,000) are the only group that clearly exceeds 100% (mean 236%, median 194% in 2023), while medium, large and major municipalities cluster below it (medians of roughly 54–89%). This size gradient motivates the regression in Section 5.

4 Statistical inference

4.1 Is mean attainment different from 100%?

Let μ be the true mean attainment rate across Ontario’s targeted municipalities. For each year I test H₀: μ = 100% against H₁: μ ≠ 100% at α = 0.05, and report a 95% confidence interval for μ three ways: the classical t-interval, a bootstrap BCa interval (10,000 resamples of the 50 municipalities), and, as a check that is robust to skew and outliers, a bootstrap interval for the median and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

Table 8. Mean attainment: confidence intervals and tests against 100%.
Year Mean Median t-interval (95%) Bootstrap BCa (95%) Bootstrap median (95%) t-test p Wilcoxon p
2023 120.5 88.5 [89.8, 151.1] [97.7, 159.9] [73.8, 109.8] 0.186 0.854
2024 97.7 78.4 [73.9, 121.6] [80.1, 128.7] [60.2, 90.1] 0.849 0.052

Interpretation. In 2023 the sample mean is 120.5% with a 95% t-interval of [89.8, 151.1]; in 2024 it is 97.7% ([73.9, 121.6]). Both intervals contain 100%, and the tests agree (t-test p = 0.186 and 0.849), so we cannot reject H₀ in either year: the data do not show that the average municipality systematically over- or under-shoots its target. The bootstrap BCa intervals ([97.7, 159.9] and [80.1, 128.7]) are shifted to the right of the t-intervals, which reflects the right skew, but they too contain 100%, so the conclusion does not hinge on normality. The typical municipality tells a somewhat different story: the Wilcoxon test gives p = 0.854 for 2023 and p = 0.052 for 2024, and the bootstrap interval for the 2024 median, [60.2, 90.1], lies entirely below 100%. In 2024 the median municipality, unlike the mean, did fall short of its target.

Two ways to “average”. The unweighted mean of municipal rates (120.5% in 2023) is higher than the aggregate rate (96.7%). The mean gives a small town the same weight as Toronto, and small towns have the largest percentages; the aggregate weights by target size. Both answers are valid but answer different questions: “how does the typical municipality do?” versus “how many of the province’s targeted homes were started?”

4.2 Did attainment change between 2023 and 2024?

Because the same 50 municipalities appear in both years, I use a paired comparison on the difference Δ = attainment₂₀₂₃ − attainment₂₀₂₄. H₀: mean Δ = 0 vs H₁: mean Δ ≠ 0 (two-sided, α = 0.05; the direction was not assumed in advance).

Table 9. Paired comparison of 2023 and 2024 attainment (percentage points).
Test Estimate 95% CI p-value
Paired t-test (mean Δ) 22.7 [-2.1, 47.6] 0.072
Wilcoxon signed-rank (median Δ) 11.3 – 0.070
Bootstrap BCa (mean Δ) 22.7 [0.2, 48.8] –
Bootstrap percentile (mean Δ) 22.7 [-0.8, 47.6] –

Interpretation. Attainment fell by 22.7 percentage points on average (30 of 50 municipalities declined). The paired t-test gives p = 0.072 and its 95% interval [-2.1, 47.6] just includes 0; the Wilcoxon test gives p = 0.070. The bootstrap intervals sit right on the boundary (BCa [0.2, 48.8], percentile [-0.8, 47.6]). At the 5% level the t-test and Wilcoxon test therefore fail to reject H₀, but the bootstrap and the p-values near 0.07 say the decline is borderline, not clearly absent: the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive. The effect size is small (Cohen’s d_z = 0.26), and with only 50 municipalities and large between-municipality variation, power to detect a change of this size is limited. Figure 6 shows why: many lines fall but many rise, and individual swings (note the log scale) are often larger than the average shift.

5 Regression: does target size predict attainment?

5.1 Choosing the model

Figure 7 plots attainment against the annual target on log–log axes. Larger targets go with lower attainment, and the relationship is close to a straight line on these axes.

I compare three specifications for each year. Attainment is strictly positive and right-skewed, so modelling its logarithm is natural, and a log of the target tames the huge range of target sizes (about 70 to 24,000 units).

Table 10. Candidate regression models (response on the scale shown; n = 50 per year).
Year Model Slope p-value R² Adj. R² Shapiro-Wilk p (residuals)
2023 A. % ~ target (linear) -0.00382 0.388 0.016 -0.005 < 0.001
2023 B. % ~ log(target) (semi-log) -44.9 < 0.001 0.269 0.254 < 0.001
2023 C. log(%) ~ log(target) (log-log) -0.252 0.002 0.185 0.168 0.792
2024 A. % ~ target (linear) -0.00332 0.272 0.025 0.005 < 0.001
2024 B. % ~ log(target) (semi-log) -32.5 < 0.001 0.233 0.217 < 0.001
2024 C. log(%) ~ log(target) (log-log) -0.206 0.012 0.126 0.108 0.530

The straight-line model A (the natural first try) has essentially no explanatory power and a non-significant slope. Model B (semi-log) shows a significant slope, but its residuals are clearly non-normal (Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.001 in both years) and it is dominated by one point: Chatham-Kent has a Cook’s distance of 1.14 in 2023 (a value above 1 is a conventional warning sign). Model C, log-log, has residuals consistent with normality, a slope with a clean interpretation (an elasticity), and, as Section 6 shows, the best out-of-sample accuracy. I therefore use it as the primary model. (R² values are not comparable across models A–B and C because the response is on a different scale; Model B’s higher R² partly reflects the influence of a few extreme values.)

Figure 8. Diagnostics for the 2023 log-log model. Residuals show no funnel shape (the smoother bends only mildly), points follow the Q–Q line, and no observation has a Cook’s distance near 1 (largest: Toronto, then Chatham-Kent).

5.2 Results and interpretation

The fitted model is log(attainment %) = β₀ + β₁ · log(annual target).

Table 11. Log-log regression of attainment on annual target, by year.
Year Slope (elasticity) 95% CI Bootstrap 95% CI p-value R² Doubling the target → Slope excl. Chatham-Kent Slope excl. Toronto
2023 -0.252 [-0.406, -0.098] [-0.432, -0.077] 0.002 0.185 -16.0% attainment -0.206 -0.317
2024 -0.206 [-0.364, -0.048] [-0.356, -0.041] 0.012 0.126 -13.3% attainment -0.171 -0.247
  • Slope. The 2023 slope is -0.252 (95% CI [-0.406, -0.098]; p = 0.002). Because both variables are logged, it is an elasticity: a 1% larger annual target goes with about 0.25% lower attainment. Equivalently, doubling a municipality’s target multiplies its attainment by 2^-0.252 ≈ 0.84, a 16% reduction. For 2024 the slope is -0.206 (95% CI [-0.364, -0.048]; p = 0.012), a 13% reduction per doubling. The two years’ intervals overlap heavily, so the strength of the relationship is similar.
  • Units scale less than proportionally with the target. Since log(attainment) = log(units) − log(target), the units started scale as target^0.75 in 2023. A municipality with a target 10% larger started only about 7.4% more homes, which is exactly why larger targets are harder to fill proportionally.
  • Intercept. β₀ = 6.22 is the predicted log-attainment at a target of one unit, an extrapolation far outside the data (smallest annual target: 73), so it carries no practical interpretation.
  • Fit. R² = 0.185 in 2023 (0.126 in 2024). Target size explains roughly one-fifth of the variation in attainment: a real but far-from-complete explanation.
  • Robustness. The bootstrap interval ([-0.432, -0.077]) is nearly identical to the classical one, and the slope is stable when single extreme observations are dropped: without Toronto (the highest Cook’s distance in this model, 0.42) the 2023 slope is -0.317 (p < 0.001), and without Chatham-Kent (the highest attainment rate) it is -0.206 (p = 0.010). Both remain negative and significant.

Caveats on the regression. (1) The target appears in the denominator of the response, so very small targets mechanically produce volatile percentages; part of the pattern is a statistical artefact of ratios, which is why the units-scaling view above is a useful complement. (2) This is an observational association across 50 municipalities, not a causal effect: targets were assigned from population and growth trends, and larger municipalities differ in many other ways (land supply, approvals, market conditions) that are not in the data.

6 Cross-validation

In-sample fit can flatter a model. To estimate out-of-sample accuracy, I use repeated 5-fold cross-validation (50 repetitions with different random fold assignments, equal-sized folds) on the 2023 data, and compare each regression with a baseline that always predicts the training-set mean. Errors are measured in attainment percentage points on the original scale (the log-log predictions are back-transformed with Duan’s smearing correction). As a stricter test, each model fitted on 2023 is also used to predict 2024, a genuine hold-out year.

Table 12. Cross-validated prediction error (percentage points of attainment). Lower is better.
Model RMSE (mean) RMSE (SD over repeats) MAE (mean) RMSE vs. baseline MAE vs. baseline RMSE (2024 hold-out) MAE (2024 hold-out)
Intercept only (mean) 108.9 1.3 72.4 +0.0% +0.0% 86.0 64.8
A. Linear: target 114.3 4.7 76.7 +4.9% +5.9% 84.8 63.7
B. Semi-log: log(target) 98.3 2.9 67.9 -9.7% -6.3% 76.2 62.7
C. Log-log 93.7 2.5 61.5 -14.0% -15.1% 70.7 53.6

Interpretation. The log-log model (C) has the lowest error: a cross-validated RMSE of 93.7 points versus 108.9 for the baseline (-14.0%), and a mean absolute error 15.1% lower. It also wins on the 2024 hold-out (RMSE 70.7 vs 86.0 for the baseline), showing the pattern carries over to a new year. The raw linear model (A) is worse than the baseline in repeated CV (+4.9%) and only marginally better on the 2024 hold-out (84.8 vs 86.0): it chases outliers, a weakness its in-sample output hides. The gains are real but moderate: a typical prediction error of roughly 94 points is still large next to the data’s scale (SD ≈ 108), consistent with an R² near 0.2.

7 Conclusions

Answering the research questions

  1. Are targets being met? Mostly not. In 2023, 20 of 50 municipalities exceeded their annual target, 12 were on track and 18 were below 80%; in 2024 these became 15, 10 and 25. In aggregate, the 50 municipalities reached 96.7% of their 2023 target and 74.2% of their 2024 target.
  2. What is the average attainment, and does it differ from 100%? The mean is 120.5% (2023) and 97.7% (2024), but neither is statistically different from 100% (p = 0.186 and 0.849); the mean is inflated by a few small municipalities, and the median municipality sits at 88% and 78%. The 2023→2024 decline of about 22.7 points is borderline (paired t-test p = 0.072; the bootstrap interval just excludes zero).
  3. Is target size related to attainment? Yes: larger targets are associated with significantly lower attainment (log-log slope -0.25 in 2023, -0.21 in 2024). Doubling a target goes with roughly a 16% lower attainment rate, and cross-validation shows the relationship improves prediction out of sample.

The takeaway: the municipalities carrying the largest absolute targets, which matter most for the 1.5-million-home goal, are the ones least likely to meet them in proportion.

Limitations. Only 50 municipalities and two years of data, so tests have limited power; the 2024 definition of “progress” is broader than 2023’s; the data count starts and not completions; annual targets ramp up; and the regression is associational. Natural extensions are adding 2025 data when available, modelling units started directly with a count model (e.g. Poisson / negative binomial with log-target offset), and adding controls such as population growth.

Appendix: Full source code

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.path = "figures/", fig.align = "center",
  fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.3, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%"
)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(boot)

source("R/load_data.R")

set.seed(57)                       # every random step below is reproducible
B_BOOT <- 10000                    # bootstrap resamples
CV_K   <- 5                        # folds
CV_REP <- 50                       # CV repetitions

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.title.position = "plot",
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "bottom")
)
status_cols <- c("Not met" = "#C0392B", "On track" = "#E69F00", "Exceeded" = "#1B9E77")

f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
fp <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste0("p = ", sprintf("%.3f", p)))   # "p = 0.072" / "p < 0.001"
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("[%.", d, "f, %.", d, "f]"), lo, hi)
long <- load_housing(use_online = FALSE)   # bundled copies of the official CSVs
wide <- make_wide(long)                    # 50 municipalities, both years side by side
tidy <- long |>
  filter(!is_aggregate) |>
  left_join(select(wide, municipality, size_class), by = "municipality") |>
  mutate(status = factor(status, levels = names(status_cols)),
         year_f = factor(year))
## ---------- 0. data-quality checks -------------------------------------------
status_rule <- function(p) cut(p, c(-Inf, 80, 100, Inf),
                               labels = names(status_cols), right = FALSE)
checks <- tibble(
  Check = c("Published % equals units ÷ annual target (±0.05 pp)",
            "Published status follows the 80% / 100% rule",
            "Cumulative 2024 − 2024 units = cumulative 2023 (all 50)",
            "Municipality names unique after trimming whitespace"),
  Result = c(
    all(abs(long$annual_units / long$annual_target * 100 - long$progress_pct) < 0.05),
    all(as.character(status_rule(tidy$progress_pct)) == as.character(tidy$status)),
    all(wide$cum_progress_since_2022_2024 - wide$annual_units_2024 ==
          wide$cum_progress_since_2022_2023),
    !any(duplicated(wide$municipality))
  )
) |> mutate(Result = ifelse(Result, "Pass", "FAIL"))

## ---------- 3. inference on the mean attainment --------------------------------
infer_mean <- function(x, yr) {
  tt  <- t.test(x, mu = 100)
  wt  <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(x, mu = 100, exact = FALSE))
  bm  <- boot(x, function(d, i) mean(d[i]), R = B_BOOT)
  bmd <- boot(x, function(d, i) median(d[i]), R = B_BOOT)
  bci <- boot.ci(bm,  type = "bca")$bca[4:5]
  mci <- boot.ci(bmd, type = "perc")$percent[4:5]
  tibble(Year = yr, Mean = mean(x), Median = median(x),
         `t-interval (95%)` = ci_txt(tt$conf.int[1], tt$conf.int[2]),
         `Bootstrap BCa (95%)` = ci_txt(bci[1], bci[2]),
         `Bootstrap median (95%)` = ci_txt(mci[1], mci[2]),
         `t-test p` = tt$p.value, `Wilcoxon p` = wt$p.value,
         t_lo = tt$conf.int[1], t_hi = tt$conf.int[2], b_lo = bci[1], b_hi = bci[2])
}
inf_tab <- bind_rows(infer_mean(wide$progress_pct_2023, 2023),
                     infer_mean(wide$progress_pct_2024, 2024))
i23 <- inf_tab |> filter(Year == 2023); i24 <- inf_tab |> filter(Year == 2024)

                                     paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE))

bdci  <- bci_all$bca[4:5]
bpci  <- bci_all$percent[4:5]

## ---------- 4. regression ------------------------------------------------------
fit_year <- function(yr) {
  d <- tidy |> filter(year == yr) |>
    transmute(municipality, target = annual_target, units = annual_units, y = progress_pct)
  list(data = d,
       lin    = lm(y ~ target, d),
       semi   = lm(y ~ log(target), d),
       loglog = lm(log(y) ~ log(target), d))
}
fits <- list(`2023` = fit_year(2023), `2024` = fit_year(2024))

mod_row <- function(m, label, yr) {
  s <- summary(m)
  tibble(Year = yr, Model = label,
         Slope = format(signif(coef(m)[2], 3), scientific = FALSE),
         `p-value` = fp(s$coefficients[2, 4]),
         `R²` = s$r.squared, `Adj. R²` = s$adj.r.squared,
         `Shapiro-Wilk p (residuals)` = fp(shapiro.test(resid(m))$p.value))
}
model_cmp <- bind_rows(lapply(c("2023", "2024"), function(y) {
  f <- fits[[y]]
  bind_rows(mod_row(f$lin,    "A. % ~ target (linear)",           y),
            mod_row(f$semi,   "B. % ~ log(target) (semi-log)",    y),
            mod_row(f$loglog, "C. log(%) ~ log(target) (log-log)", y))
}))

cook <- cooks.distance(fits[["2023"]]$semi)
top_cook <- names(which.max(cook))
top_cook_name <- fits[["2023"]]$data$municipality[as.integer(top_cook)]
top_cook_val  <- max(cook)

slope_boot <- function(d) {
  b <- boot(d, function(dd, i) coef(lm(log(y) ~ log(target), dd[i, ]))[2], R = 5000)
  boot.ci(b, type = "perc")$percent[4:5]
}
loglog_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(c("2023", "2024"), function(y) {
  f <- fits[[y]]; m <- f$loglog; s <- summary(m)
  ci <- confint(m)[2, ]; bci <- slope_boot(f$data)
  nk <- f$data |> filter(municipality != "Chatham-Kent")
  m_nk <- lm(log(y) ~ log(target), nk)
  nt <- f$data |> filter(municipality != "Toronto")
  m_nt <- lm(log(y) ~ log(target), nt)
  tibble(Year = y,
         `Slope (elasticity)` = coef(m)[2],
         `95% CI` = ci_txt(ci[1], ci[2], 3),
         `Bootstrap 95% CI` = ci_txt(bci[1], bci[2], 3),
         `p-value` = fp(s$coefficients[2, 4]),
         `R²` = s$r.squared,
         `Doubling the target →` = sprintf("%+.1f%% attainment", 100 * (2^coef(m)[2] - 1)),
         `Slope excl. Chatham-Kent` = coef(m_nk)[2],
         p_nk = summary(m_nk)$coefficients[2, 4],
         `Slope excl. Toronto` = coef(m_nt)[2],
         p_nt = summary(m_nt)$coefficients[2, 4],
         `Units scale as target^` = coef(m)[2] + 1,
         lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2])
}))

## ---------- 5. cross-validation -------------------------------------------------
cv_models <- list(
  "Intercept only (mean)"   = function(tr) { m <- mean(tr$y);            function(nd) rep(m, nrow(nd)) },
  "A. Linear: target"       = function(tr) { m <- lm(y ~ target, tr);    function(nd) predict(m, nd) },
  "B. Semi-log: log(target)"= function(tr) { m <- lm(y ~ log(target), tr); function(nd) predict(m, nd) },
  "C. Log-log"              = function(tr) {
    m <- lm(log(y) ~ log(target), tr); smear <- mean(exp(resid(m)))   # Duan smearing
    function(nd) exp(predict(m, nd)) * smear }
)
d_cv <- fits[["2023"]]$data
cv_raw <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(CV_REP), function(r) {
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(CV_K), length.out = nrow(d_cv)))      # equal-sized folds
  bind_rows(lapply(names(cv_models), function(nm) {
    pred <- numeric(nrow(d_cv))
    for (k in seq_len(CV_K)) {
      pred[fold == k] <- cv_models[[nm]](d_cv[fold != k, ])(d_cv[fold == k, ])
    }
    tibble(rep = r, Model = nm, RMSE = sqrt(mean((d_cv$y - pred)^2)), MAE = mean(abs(d_cv$y - pred)))
  }))
}))
cv_tab <- cv_raw |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  summarise(`RMSE (mean)` = mean(RMSE), `RMSE (SD over repeats)` = sd(RMSE),
            `MAE (mean)` = mean(MAE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = names(cv_models))) |>
  arrange(Model)
base_rmse <- cv_tab$`RMSE (mean)`[1]
base_mae  <- cv_tab$`MAE (mean)`[1]
cv_tab <- cv_tab |>
  mutate(`RMSE vs. baseline` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (`RMSE (mean)` / base_rmse - 1)),
         `MAE vs. baseline`  = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (`MAE (mean)`  / base_mae  - 1)))

d24_new <- fits[["2024"]]$data   # temporal hold-out: fit on 2023, predict 2024
oot <- bind_rows(lapply(names(cv_models), function(nm) {
  p <- cv_models[[nm]](d_cv)(d24_new)
  tibble(Model = nm, `RMSE (2024 hold-out)` = sqrt(mean((d24_new$y - p)^2)),
         `MAE (2024 hold-out)` = mean(abs(d24_new$y - p)))
}))
cv_tab <- left_join(cv_tab, oot, by = "Model")
